title: Liver blood tests
subtitle: Bilirubin, ALT, ALP, GGT, albumin and synthetic function
summary: Bilirubin, ALT, ALP, GGT, albumin and synthetic function
introduction: “LFTs” contain markers of hepatocyte injury, cholestasis and synthetic function. ALT, ALP and bilirubin describe patterns of injury; albumin and INR help assess synthetic function but are influenced by other conditions.

rows.name: ALT
rows.referenceRange: Laboratory and sex dependent; often upper limit about 35–50 IU/L
highInterpretation: Hepatocellular injury. Causes include fatty liver disease, viral hepatitis, alcohol-related injury, medicines, ischaemia and autoimmune hepatitis.

rows.name: ALP
lowInterpretation: Can occur with malnutrition, zinc deficiency, hypothyroidism or rare metabolic disorders.
highInterpretation: Cholestasis or biliary obstruction, but also bone disease, healing fracture, pregnancy and growth. Use GGT to support hepatic origin.

rows.name: GGT
highInterpretation: Supports hepatic origin of raised ALP. Can rise with alcohol, cholestasis, fatty liver and enzyme-inducing medicines; it is non-specific.

rows.name: Bilirubin
highInterpretation: Pre-hepatic haemolysis, hepatocellular dysfunction or biliary obstruction. Visible jaundice often appears around 40–60 micromol/L but varies.

rows.name: Albumin
lowInterpretation: Chronic liver dysfunction, inflammation, malnutrition, renal or gastrointestinal protein loss, or dilution. It changes slowly and is not a sensitive marker of acute liver injury.
highInterpretation: Usually haemoconcentration from reduced plasma volume.

rows.name: INR / prothrombin time
rows.referenceRange: Use local range; interpret separately when taking warfarin
highInterpretation: Can indicate reduced hepatic synthesis, vitamin K deficiency, anticoagulant effect or DIC. In acute liver injury, a rising INR is an important marker of failure.

rows.name: Hepatocellular pattern
highInterpretation: Consider viral, metabolic, autoimmune, drug-induced or ischaemic hepatocyte injury.

rows.name: Cholestatic pattern
rows.referenceRange: ALP rise predominates, often with GGT and bilirubin
highInterpretation: Consider gallstone obstruction, biliary infection, pancreatic/biliary malignancy, drug-induced cholestasis or infiltrative disease.

rows.name: Mixed pattern
rows.referenceRange: Both ALT and ALP substantially raised
highInterpretation: Consider drug injury, infection, obstruction with hepatocyte injury or another mixed hepatic process.

rows.name: Isolated bilirubin rise
rows.referenceRange: Other enzymes normal or minimally changed
highInterpretation: Consider Gilbert syndrome, haemolysis or an early/partial obstructive process; assess conjugated fraction where available.

urgentFindings: Jaundice with fever, right-upper-quadrant pain, hypotension or new confusion: consider ascending cholangitis and urgent hospital assessment.
Acute liver injury with confusion, drowsiness, hypoglycaemia, bleeding, rising INR or metabolic acidosis: consider acute liver failure.
Very large new ALT rise, particularly into the thousands, with hypotension, overdose risk, medication change or viral symptoms.
Raised bilirubin with pale stool, dark urine, pruritus, weight loss or a palpable gallbladder requires prompt obstructive/malignancy assessment.
Albumin alone should not be used to diagnose acute liver failure; check INR, glucose, mental state and the overall clinical picture.
overrides: Use the reporting laboratory’s reference ranges and compare with previous results, symptoms, observations, medication and fluid status.
